response.answer: Full radiative flux methods with low-albedo and high-emissivity assumptions minimize bias in dense urban canyons for Tmrt computation. High-albedo materials and reflective walls improve thermal comfort. Low ground albedo complements high wall albedo in urban design.

results.title: The simple urban radiation model for estimating mean radiant temperature in idealised street canyons - ScienceDirect
results.content: ## Urban Climate. Volume 35, January 2021, 100694. # The simple urban radiation model for estimating mean radiant temperature in idealised street canyons. Author links open overlay panel. Under a Creative Commons license. ## Abstract. Thermal comfort is an important component of health-related urban well-being (UrbWellth) of the urban population. Outdoors in sunny conditions the human thermal environment is strongly influenced by radiation fluxes, which are often expressed as a mean radiant temperature (Tmrt). In an urban environment Tmrt is, especially in sunny conditions, strongly influenced by the building morphology due to shading and reflection of radiation. To model these morphological effects within an urban system model for UrbWellth, a simple model for Tmrt is required that simplifies the actual urban environment to reduce computational costs but still considers the most important aspects of Tmrt variability within a city. To do so, within this paper the open-source and modular Simple Urban Radiation Model (SURM) is presented. SURM is validated with respect to different calculation methods of both view factors and radiative fluxes as well as to radiation modification by buildings. The results indicate that SURM models radiative fluxes and radiative influences of buildings sufficiently accurate to be applicable as one component of an urban system model for sunny conditions. ## Keywords. ## Cited by (0). : Present address: Technical University of Denmark, Department of Wind Energy, Risø Campus, Frederiksborgvej 399, 4000 Roskilde, Denmark. Published by Elsevier B.V.

results.title: Optimizing pedestrian thermal comfort in urban street canyons for summer and winter: Tree planting or low-albedo pavements? - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Optimizing pedestrian thermal comfort in urban street canyons for summer and winter: Tree planting or low-albedo pavements? This study systematically investigated the effect of different albedo pavements on thermal comfort in street canyons using albedo measurements, experimental data, and simulations, factoring in tree cover and seasonal variations. These findings suggest urban planners prioritize tree planting for its cooling effects in densely populated areas, and use low-albedo materials in open, unshaded areas to reduce reflected radiation and enhance comfort. Pedestrian thermal comfort in street canyons is influenced by multiple factors such as geometry, building surfaces characteristics, albedo, and greenery: Firstly, streets with higher aspect ratios—meaning the ratio of building height to street width (H/W) is larger, resulting in narrower and deeper street canyons—have better wind speeds and increased shading in summer (Muniz-Gäal et al., 2020). A substantial body of research has demonstrated that high-albedo materials effectively mitigate the UHI effect by reducing solar radiation absorption, consequently lowering surface and air temperatures (Ta), and improving human thermal comfort. However, some studies indicate that while high-albedo materials regulate the microclimate, they may paradoxically increase heat stress by reflecting solar radiation, thereby elevating mean radiant temperature (*Tmrt*) and PET (Cui et al., 2022), and consequently reducing thermal comfort (Jung, 2024; Gapski et al., 2023; Salvati et al., 2022). During summer, one of the key mechanisms is transpiration, where tree leaves release moisture, reducing ambient heat and improving thermal comfort in urban canyons (Huang et al., 2022). Overall, the benefits of tree shading in reducing thermal radiation and regulating temperature outweigh the drawbacks of reduced wind speed (Zheng et al., 2025), ultimately enhancing thermal comfort and providing significant benefits for urban street canyon environments. However, research comparing the efficacy of tree planting versus albedo adjustment in optimizing thermal comfort remains limited, with the majority of studies focusing on summer heat wave periods. This study utilized a combination of experiments and simulations to analyze 120 scenario combinations, investigating the effects of surface material albedo and tree planting on pedestrian thermal comfort in urban canyons. ### Effects of urban tree planting on thermal comfort and air quality in the street canyon in a subtropical climate. Assessing the impact of street tree health on urban thermal regulation and pedestrian comfort.

results.title: A mathematical model for rapid estimation of solar radiation in urban canyons with trees and its applications - ScienceDirect
results.content: # A mathematical model for rapid estimation of solar radiation in urban canyons with trees and its applications. A rapid and robust street canyon radiation model with trees is developed. A flexible and robust mathematical model for solar radiation in urban canyons is proposed in this study to estimate solar radiation potential at the street level quickly and can be applied to the urban scale. The newly developed model considers the effect of trees on street canyon radiative transfer based on some assumptions and simplifications. Using the matrix method to resolve the infinite number of multi-reflections, the model accurately predicts solar radiation inside the street canyon compared to experimental data. In recent years, various street canyon radiation models have been established to estimate urban canyon effective albedo [12], [13], [14], [15], solar radiation distribution [16], [17], [18], [19], and mean radiant temperature [20], [21]. The second category of urban canyon radiation models refers to those that express the location and size of trees explicitly in the street canyon. When trees are present in street canyons, calculating view factors between built surfaces becomes an obstacle to model development. Existing explicit urban canyon radiation models use this approach to deal with radiative transfer between trees and street canyon surfaces [16], [19], [27]. Considering the shading effect of trees, and combining it with the matrix algorithm for infinite radiative reflection and the heat transmission of the building envelope, a new modeling framework of radiative transfer in street canyons with trees was developed. In view of the limitations of the existing methods, the present work aims to develop a real practical urban canyon radiation model. Adopting the matrix method for infinite radiative reflections, a novel modeling framework is developed to capture the solar radiation balance inside a street canyon. This study develops a real practical multiple-layer urban canyon radiation model for evaluating solar potential on street and urban scales. Using the matrix method to resolve the infinite number of reflections, the proposed model can accurately and rapidly predict solar radiation inside the street canyon. ### A single-layer urban canopy model with transmissive radiation exchange between trees and street canyons.

results.title: Relevance of Ground and Wall Albedo for Outdoor Thermal Comfort in Tropical Savanna Climates: Evidence from Parametric Simulations
results.content: albedo; outdoor thermal comfort; sustainable urban design; tropical savanna; parametric simulations; ground material; wall materials. While much of the existing research focuses on radiative effects or temperature-based metrics, fewer studies have explored how material choices—such as wall and ground albedo—directly influence human thermal comfort in outdoor urban environments, particularly in tropical savanna climates, where intense solar radiation and rapid urbanization amplify heat stress [32]. This study poses the following question: how do ground and wall albedo independently and interactively affect pedestrian thermal comfort (UTCI) in tropical savanna urban canyons, and what material combinations optimize sustainable urban design for heat mitigation and livability? This study employed parametric simulations to evaluate ground and wall albedo effects on pedestrian thermal comfort in tropical savanna climates, aiming to inform sustainable urban design by optimizing material selections for heat mitigation and livability. The study used parametric simulations to evaluate ground and wall albedo effects on pedestrian thermal comfort in tropical savanna climates, measured via the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI). This study, measuring pedestrian thermal comfort via the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) in tropical savanna climates, found that ground albedo (0.2–0.8) had a minimal impact (mean UTCI amplitude 0.44 °C), while wall albedo (0.05–0.90) significantly reduced the UTCI (up to −2.80 °C), with emissivity fixed at 0.9 for all materials. As far as urban design and surface material choice are concerned, the results presented in this paper imply the following: (1) the emphasis should be less on ground materials and more attention should be paid to wall material selection for effective heat mitigation during tropical savanna summers; (2) particularly in a highly reflective wall environment, it would be preferable to maintain low ground albedo to avoid offsetting the cooling impact of the highly reflective walls; for instance, urban designers could prioritize reflective wall coatings (e.g., white paints, albedo ~0.8) paired with low-albedo asphalt (albedo ~0.2) to maximize cooling in deep canyons, optimizing cost-effectiveness. For urban designers, instead of directly assuming that higher wall albedo would have better heat mitigation, numerical simulations, as employed in this study, are critical for evaluating the effect of wall material choices on outdoor thermal comfort, ensuring optimal outcomes in tropical savanna climates.

results.title: White Limestone Albedo: UHI Mitigation Data & Metrics
results.content: **Citadel Stone white limestone outdoor tiles**' high solar reflectance reduces surface temperatures substantially compared to conventional dark pavements, contributing to urban heat island mitigation at site and district scales. High-albedo surfaces like white limestone reflect most solar energy back to the atmosphere, preventing conversion to sensible heat that would otherwise warm the surface and surrounding air. **Credible outputs:** Surface temperature maps showing spatial distribution of heating/cooling across the modeled domain, near-surface air temperature differences (typically reported at pedestrian height) between baseline and high-albedo scenarios, and thermal comfort indices like Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) or Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) that integrate temperature, humidity, wind and radiation. **Adjacency effects and radiation trapping:** In dense urban canyons with high building facades, high-albedo ground surfaces reflect solar radiation upward where it may be absorbed by building walls, reducing the net cooling benefit. **Snippet:** The albedo effect is surface reflectivity; white limestone’s high reflectance returns more solar energy, lowering surface temperatures and reducing heat radiated into urban air.
